thread.title: Special Participation B: Cursor Composer on HW 2 Coding
thread.content: For this assignment, I tackled the coding questions on HW 2 using Cursor Composer, which is a language model specifically designed for software engineering and code generation tasks (released in late October of this year). The IDE I used for this assignment was Cursor, which is the primary way of accessing this model. The link to my annotated transcript of my conversation with the model can be found here.Here is a brief summary of my interactions with the model: it is very strong at code generation and reasoning. It can definitely one-shot most questions in the homework. However, it is much less reliable when answers depend on actually seeing plots / running code, and it sometimes overstates what it has “looked at” or “run.” The model did very well when the problem was well-specified mathematically and didn’t require actually seeing outputs. Examples:Implementing SGD+Momentum, RMSProp, Adam in optim.py.Implementing He initialization, zero initialization, and gradient norm logging.Implementing gradient ascent step (gd_step), Monte-Carlo smoothing (smoothed_f), finite-difference gradient step, etc.However, when questions explicitly said “answer based on the plot / visualization,” the model often:Answered using generic theory rather than the actual plot, even while saying things like:“Reviewing the notebook section with the gradient norm plot…”“Updating the answer to match the plot…”Produced initial answers that didn’t match the actual plotsOnly after being challenged (“Are you sure? That doesn’t match…”) did it admit it had not actually run the code or seen the plot.Takeaway: although the model capabilities are quite impressive, the outputs still have to be read carefully to make sure it's answering honestly. Additionally, I noticed that it had a tendency to give somewhat verbose responses for conceptual questions, repeating the same idea several times in different language.
thread.document:
For this assignment, I tackled the coding questions on HW 2 using Cursor Composer, which is a language model specifically designed for software engineering and code generation tasks (released in late October of this year). The IDE I used for this assignment was Cursor, which is the primary way of accessing this model. 

The link to my annotated transcript of my conversation with the model can be found here.

Here is a brief summary of my interactions with the model: it is very strong at code generation  and reasoning. It can definitely one-shot most questions in the homework. However, it is much  less reliable when answers depend on actually seeing plots / running code, and it sometimes overstates what it has “looked at” or “run.” 

The model did very well when the problem was well-specified mathematically and didn’t require actually seeing outputs. Examples:

Implementing SGD+Momentum, RMSProp, Adam in optim.py.

Implementing He initialization, zero initialization, and gradient norm logging.

Implementing gradient ascent step (gd_step), Monte-Carlo smoothing (smoothed_f), finite-difference gradient step, etc.

However, when questions explicitly said “answer based on the plot / visualization,” the model often:

Answered using generic theory rather than the actual plot, even while saying things like:

“Reviewing the notebook section with the gradient norm plot…”

“Updating the answer to match the plot…”

Produced initial answers that didn’t match the actual plots

Only after being challenged (“Are you sure? That doesn’t match…”) did it admit it had not actually run the code or seen the plot.

Takeaway: although the model capabilities are quite impressive, the outputs still have to be read carefully to make sure it's answering honestly. Additionally, I noticed that it had a tendency to give somewhat verbose responses for conceptual questions, repeating the same idea several times in different language.
